sources.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does the LORD require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

In Micah 6:6-8 the prophet answers the question of what offering would please God. Rather than more sacrifices, the passage stresses justice, faithful kindness and humility before God. The Hebrew word often translated “mercy” (hesed) carries the sense of loyal, covenant love.

answer: Micah 6:8 sums up what God asks in three phrases: “to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God” [S1]. According to the commentary, the verse answers the question of what offering would please God, and instead of more sacrifices it points to justice, faithful kindness and humility before God [S2]. The commentary also notes that the Hebrew word often translated “mercy” (hesed) carries the sense of loyal, covenant love [S2].

sources.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

Paul contrasts the “works of the flesh” (Galatians 5:19-21) with the fruit of the Spirit. The singular word “fruit” is often read as describing one unified character produced by the Spirit rather than nine separate gifts.

inputs.question: What is the fruit of the Spirit?

answer: Paul lists the fruit of the Spirit as “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control,” and adds, “Against such things there is no law” [S1]. The commentary notes that Paul sets this list against the “works of the flesh,” and that the singular word “fruit” is often read as one unified character the Spirit produces rather than nine separate gifts [S2].

sources.text: Then Peter came and said to him, “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? Until seven times?” Jesus said to him, “I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.

The expression is generally understood as an unlimited number.

recent_messages.content: What did Jesus teach about anger?
Jesus links anger with murder in the Sermon on the Mount [S1].

inputs.question: Why did Jesus say forgive seventy times seven?

answer: Peter suggested forgiving “until seven times,” and Jesus answered “until seventy times seven” [S1]. The commentary notes that the expression is generally understood as an unlimited number, so the point is not to keep count at all [S3]. Jesus then begins a parable about the Kingdom of Heaven, “like a certain king who wanted to settle accounts with his servants” [S2]. The supplied sources do not give further historical background on the saying.

sources.text: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The Word became flesh and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the only born Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.

The Greek term translated “Word” is logos. In Greek thought it could mean reason or the ordering principle of the world, and in the Jewish scriptures God creates and acts by his word. John applies the title to Jesus, identifying the Word with the one who “became flesh” (John 1:14).

inputs.question: What does “the Word” mean in John 1?

answer: In the text itself, John says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” [S1], and later, “The Word became flesh and lived among us” [S2]. The commentary explains that the Greek term is logos, which in Greek thought could mean reason or the ordering principle of the world, while in the Jewish scriptures God creates and acts by his word [S3]. John applies the title to Jesus, the one who “became flesh” [S2][S3].

sources.text: Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil;

Paul wrote 1 Corinthians to a church divided over leaders, status and spiritual gifts. Chapter 13 sits between two chapters on spiritual gifts (chapters 12 and 14) and describes the love that should govern how those gifts are used.

inputs.question: What did Paul mean by “love is patient”?

answer: “Love is patient and is kind” opens a list describing what love does and does not do: it doesn’t envy, brag or seek its own way, is not provoked, and “takes no account of evil” [S1]. The commentary explains the setting: Paul was writing to a church divided over leaders, status and spiritual gifts, and the chapter sits between two chapters on gifts to describe the love that should govern how they are used [S2]. Read that way, patience here is practical: bearing with others instead of competing with them. That last point is an interpretation of the passage rather than a direct statement of it.
